title: The shrewd manager (Luke 16:1–13)
hook: a puzzling story: use money to make friends; you can't serve two masters

segments.voice: Yesterday, teknon: the older brother outside the party, and a father who came out to plead. Your line was all I have is yours.

It may be the most puzzling story Jesus tells. A dishonest employee gets praised. Money gets called unrighteous, then used to make friends. Even Luke seems to feel the strain: after the story come four or five different morals, one after another. And a clue links it to the prodigal son. The younger son wasted his father's goods. This manager is accused of wasting his master's goods. Same Greek word. Two stories about what we do with what isn't really ours.

A rich man's manager is caught and told to hand in the books. He panics, and in the King James Bible talks to himself: "What shall I do? for my lord taketh away from me the stewardship: I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed." Then an idea. He calls in his master's debtors one by one. How much do you owe? A hundred measures of oil. Quick, write fifty. And you? A hundred measures of wheat. Write eighty. When he's out of a job, they'll owe him a favor. And the punchline: "the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely." Not for honesty. For being shrewd: seeing the crisis coming and acting fast. Scholars genuinely disagree about the details. Some think he cut out his own commission; others, the master's interest; others that he was simply dishonest to the end. The lesson Jesus draws is clear: use the money of this world, mammon, to make friends, because people last and money doesn't. Mammon is an Aramaic word for wealth, and Jesus treats it almost like a rival god. Then today's line: "He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much." Small things train big things. And the warning: "Ye cannot serve God and mammon." Money makes a fine servant and a terrible master. Look back at the week: Proverbs, a feast refused with excuses, a tower that needs counting, a grumble that started three stories, a son far off, another at the door, and now a manager who saw clearly that his time was short.
screen: then, large: `FAITHFUL IN THAT WHICH IS LEAST.`

segments.voice: Think about the money that passed through your hands this week, rent, food, things bought on a whim, and notice which of it made a connection with another person. Then think of someone you'd like to be closer to, or who could use a little help, and the small amount that could turn into friendship: a coffee, a shared meal, someone's bus fare.
Mammon, the Aramaic word for wealth that Jesus treats almost like a rival master: money for making friends, never the thing you serve.
Your line: faithful in little. Day five hundred sixty, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: Christians use the language of stewardship for money, time and the earth, as things held in trust; many churches teach regular giving, and some Christians keep budgets that set aside money for hospitality and helping others.

myth: Jesus praises the manager for being dishonest
the master commends him for acting wisely, shrewdly, in a crisis. not for his honesty.
Luke uses the same word for wasted here and for the younger son
both waste what wasn't theirs: the son his father's, the manager his master's.

fork.setup: you're a manager about to be fired. you can't dig and you're ashamed to beg. what do you do?
options: confess everything and hope for mercy.
cut what each debtor owes, so they'll welcome you later.
fork.reveal: he rewrites the bills, fifty for a hundred, eighty for a hundred, and the master commends him because he had done wisely.

original.note: Greek, from Aramaic: wealth, property. Jesus treats it almost like a rival master.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus approves of cooking the books.
what it means: be as clear-eyed about what lasts as this man was about his job, use money for people, and never let it be your master.
what a scholar hears: the verb for wasting links him to the prodigal, and scholars still debate whether he cut his commission, the interest, or simply cheated.
recall: gathers her brood under her wings
guess: wealth, treated almost like a rival master
a kind of manna, bread sent from heaven
a debt written down in a master's books

chat.says: Wait, Jesus praised a dishonest manager? Is he saying cheating is fine?
options: No, the master praised him for being shrewd and acting fast, not for being honest.
Yes, in that story bending the rules was fine because the master was rich.
No, he praised the debtors for paying their bills quickly and in full.
chat.meaning: The lord commended him because he had done wisely: he saw the crisis coming. Jesus still warns, ye cannot serve God and mammon.

mammon.meaning: an Aramaic word for wealth, treated like a rival master

steward.meaning: a manager who runs a rich man's affairs

notes: διασκορπίζω in Luke 15:13 and 16:1: confirm the shared verb.
The three readings (own commission, master's interest, plain dishonesty) are a standard summary of the debate. Confirm.
μαμωνᾶς from Aramaic māmōnā: standard lexicon.
'Money makes a fine servant and a terrible master' is a proverb, not scripture; spoken as commentary.
